items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Rodger Kay asking me to hurry back to New York because he was going to take a combo into a new club and wanted me to join him... The trumpet chair had been left open for me and the band had worked in the club two weeks before I returned.

ctx.x: In the meantime, I had been receiving letters and telegrams from Rodger Kay asking me to hurry back to New York because he was going to take a combo into a new club and wanted me to join him. I played my last job with Sissle in Louisville, Ky. and taken an early morning train to Cincinnati, where I stayed a couple of days to visit my parents and the rest of my family. Saw a few old friends and returned to the Apple.

Things had happened quite fast and unforunately for Rodger. He had formed an orchestra with a white drummer, Jim Chapin, a Canadian pianist whose name was Bill something, a well known white bassist named Sid Wales and Jem Davis, an alto man that had a style on the order of Pete Brown. Lem and Pete both lived in Brooklyn.

The trumpet chair had been left open for me and the band had worked in the club two weeks before I returned. The club was located at 152nd East 55th Street. But Rodger Ray was not there because Sid Weiss had pulled a trick on him. Rodger's voice was not as good as he thought it was and when Sid heard him sing, and he knew that Rodger did not belong to the musicians union because he was not a musician, he reported him and a union delegate came to the club and told Rodger he could not work, because he was not a…
